name: Kepler’s elliptical model of Mars
summary: In Astronomia nova (1609) Kepler argued that Mars moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus, replacing circles and epicycles; William Lower approved it by 1611.
description: A geometrical astronomical model in which Mars follows an ellipse around the Sun, with the Sun at one focus. This differed as a historical proposed orbit from earlier circular and epicyclic models. The 1609 publication is scoped to Mars; later extension to all planets is not bundled into the dated formulation.
tier_reason: The elliptical-orbit result supplied later celestial-mechanics reasoning and generations of orbital prediction; rank concerns the result rather than a surviving copy.

impact.note: Astronomers rebuilt planetary prediction on it, and gravitation and celestial mechanics rested on it; reach stays professional, so total 6 implies tier 1, not 0.

why: Tycho Brahe's precise observations of Mars, which Kepler inherited, could not be fitted by circular models to within their accuracy.

market.note: The node is the scientific claim and its scholarly reception, not an individually marketed product.

date.basis: The ETH catalogue and title leaf date the published Astronomia nova to 1609.

events.statement: Kepler’s Astronomia nova published an argument that the orbit of Mars is an ellipse.
events.place_note: Holy Roman Empire; place of publication
events.scope: 1609 published geometrical model of Mars moving on an elliptical solar orbit.
events.caveats: The publication date does not establish first formulation or proof of immediate acceptance. The retained pages were examined in Latin; no claim is made that all 1609 calculations were checked.

evidence.locator: Ch. LVIII, printed p. 285 / source PDF p. 332; title leaf
evidence.supports: States the ellipse conclusion and identifies the following demonstration as concerning Mars.
Clarifies that the first-law formulation in the 1609 book was explicitly restricted to Mars.

date.label: By 1611
date.basis: The surviving letter is headed 6 February 1610, but Chapman discusses whether the modern-year equivalent is 1610 or 1611; 1611 is a conservative upper bound.

events.statement: In a letter to Harriot, William Lower expressed approval of Kepler’s elliptical planetary path, referred specifically to Mars, and described reading the book with calculation.
events.scope: Lower’s response to the elliptical Mars-orbit idea in Kepler’s Astronomia nova.
applications: Scholarly reading and criticism of orbital models
events.population: William Lower; Thomas Harriot was the letter recipient
events.caveats: This is a later transcription of private correspondence, not direct inspection of the autograph, a public teaching event, proof Harriot endorsed every claim, or proof Lower had checked every calculation. Earlier acceptance or knowledge is possible.

evidence.locator: Printed pp. 120–124, Lower’s letter of 6 February
evidence.supports: Transcribes Lower’s reaction to the ellipse, his references to Mars, and his ongoing calculation and difficulties.
Historian treats the letter as evidence of Lower’s acceptance of elliptical orbits.
Discusses the 1610/1611 ambiguity and argues provisionally for the earlier year.

earliest_record.rationale: Earliest defensible dated record of this scoped referent in the retained evidence; later community entry is recorded separately. The ETH catalogue and title leaf date the published Astronomia nova to 1609. The publication date does not establish first formulation or proof of immediate acceptance. The retained pages were examined in Latin; no claim is made that all 1609 calculations were checked. This is the earliest supported record currently established here, not certification of absolute priority.

community_entry.community: William Lower, corresponding with Thomas Harriot
community_entry.rationale: Lower’s explicit response is a named independent reader’s recognition of the ellipse and is stronger than assuming that every recipient of the 1609 book accepted it.
community_entry.caveats: This is a later transcription of private correspondence, not direct inspection of the autograph, a public teaching event, proof Harriot endorsed every claim, or proof Lower had checked every calculation. Earlier acceptance or knowledge is possible.
